question: During an experiment conducted to alter the infectivity of common viruses that affect humans, an investigator successfully increases the host range of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The new strain of the virus can infect fibroblast-like cells in addition to the usual target of HIV. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the increase in the host range of the virus?

options.opa: Mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins
options.opb: Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene
options.opc: Increased rate of budding out of host cells
options.opd: Reassortment of genetic material between segments of two viruses
options.ope: Excessive activity of viral RNA polymerase

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins -> alters viral attachment and entry mechanisms -> allows infection of new cell types -> increased host range of the virus -> 85%
CHAIN: Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene -> changes viral receptor specificity -> enables infection of fibroblast-like cells -> expands host range of the virus -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely explanation for the increase in the host range of the virus is the mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins. This mutation alters viral attachment and entry mechanisms, allowing infection of new cell types, which results in an increased host range of the virus. Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene could also contribute to changes in viral receptor specificity and enable infection of fibroblast-like cells, expanding the host range. Evidence paths related to cells interacting with genes and host factors support the concept of genetic changes influencing host range expansion.
analysis: The most likely explanation for the increase in the host range of the virus aligns with the enhanced information provided, indicating that a mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins is the primary factor. This mutation alters viral attachment and entry mechanisms, enabling infection of new cell types and expanding the host range of the virus.
